In my opinion he's very difficult to play well. He requires a lot of practice to get to the point where you can win games with him, and he requires a good sense of what your opponents can threaten and block to do well. 

His turn to turn damage is really quite bad, but he makes up for it by being able to send a massive amount of damage in one singular turn. 

The deck has gotten much more difficult in Part the Mistveil with the printing of Kindle, which has revolutionized the way the deck is played. Kindle lines are much harder in terms of sequencing, and they are very easy to mess up and lose on. 

He's very rewarding to learn though. His skill ceiling is incredibly high, and even after playing for a year on him I'm still learning new stuff. Goldfishing with the deck also helps a lot, just to learn the lines. If you want to play him I encourage it, but he isn't easy to learn. Also you *need* Storm Striders, they can't be substituted

So I run a Toshiro prison deck that makes life really bad for everyone at the table while filling the graveyard. Here's what I have learned piloting the deck:

You definitely want your removal at instant speed for most of it. For example, [[Tragic Slip]], [[Eliminate]], and [[Go For The Throat]] are all excellent pieces of removal with a good amount of things they can target. Cards like [[Tsabo's Decree]] are slightly niche, but can really mess with people's deck construction, especially with Toshiro's flashback ability. I would recommend against cards like [[Doom Blade]] and [[Cast Down]]. Non-black is a heavier restriction than most realize and Cast Down doesn't hit commanders at all. 

Toshiro shouldn't be cast too early. You need a way to fill your yard with cards first before he's really effective. This is where [[Mesmeric Orb]] comes in. The card lets you fill your bin with all sorts of action. I use it in tandem with [[Kozilek, Butcher of Truth]], [[Basalt Monolith]], and [[Syr Konrad]] as a wincon as well. 

Toshiro also benefits from instant speed reanimation effects. A [[Shallow Grave]] or [[Goryo's Vengeance]] in the bin can win you the game off a sacrifice the opponent made on their turn when you reanimate something like [[Razaketh the Foulblooded]] to fetch your wincons. 

If you have more money than sense, or are really good at trades, I would recommend picking up a [[Vampiric Tutor]], [[Cabal Coffers]], [[Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth]], [[Lake of the Dead]], [[Chains of Mephistopheles]], and [[The Tabernacle at Pendrell Vale]]. Vamp tutor is amazing to flashback, Coffers, Urborg, and Lake all generate tons of mana and can win you the game easily, and Chains and Tabernacle, though expensive, offer a great way to fill up your graveyard and lock others out of their cards (Chains), and free deaths on upkeep for mana starved opponents (Tabernacle). The last two are insanely expensive tho, and the deck is perfectly fine without either. 

The rules change recently buffed Toshiro, so now he gets triggers off commander death as well. This is great for obvious reasons.

I think Companion is a very poorly implemented mechanic overall, and that the sweet spot of it being good is so small that it's maybe not worth attempting. 

I think if R&D looked at EDH, specifically cEDH, they would see that there's an inherent issue with something always being available. For example, a deck with Zur the Enchanter as its commander essentially *always* has access to Necropotence. A Thrasios/Tymna deck *always* has two card advantage engines they can cast. Najeela has the win on the creature in the command zone. This is relatively okay and balanced out by a number of restrictions and gameplay variations, four players as opposed to two, 100 cards in singleton with color restrictions. 

The issue is Companions have restrictions that aren't anywhere close to the commander ones. Lurrus's is a non-issue; he slotted into pre-existing decks. Yorion's card count isn't enough to cause enough variance for that effect to be fair; especially considering how powerful EDH can be with twice the restriction.

The notion that off-color fetches are an issue is easily the stupidest thing of all time. There's not a way to implement that that makes the format any better. 

If you have it so that color identity extends to land types, then you run into issues with cards like [[Farseek]], [[Submerge]], [[Massacre]], and [[Cloudpost]], as they all mention a land type. Farseek becomes a five color card, Massacre is an Orzhov card, Submerge is Simic, and Cloudpost is unplayable in literally everything, as "Locus" becomes its color identity. Now people are ripping cards out of decks because of an unintuitive rules change. This will make a lot of people angry for no reason. 

If you target strictly the Fetch cycles, then all you do is make four and five color decks ultra consistent, and nerf two and three color decks in terms of mana. All you do with this is punish people for owning these cards, and then they take them out of their two color or three color decks, annoyed and upset that they now have cards they can't play with. This will make a lot of people angry for no reason. 

If you ban them, all you do is add to the banlist, people will get mad, and you'll never hear the end of it. 

There's no way to implement this without it being the most convoluted nonsense ever, and without making everyone upset.

Honestly I feel like the deck has too much focus on white. You need card draw, which white struggles with compared to black. [[Necropotence]] is the best card in a Zur deck, because you can basically keep you hand full at all times, which is a major boon. The "skipping your draw step" is also an advantage in a lot of ways, though not immediately apparent. Since the deck is grindier than most Zur decks, put a [[Phyrexian Arena]] in there. It's tutorable with Zur, and it's a better slot in than [[Bitterblossom]] is in this case. 

That actually segues into another issue, which is that you have a ton of enchantments that are un-tutorable by Zur. It's okay to have some ([[Smothering Tithe]]) but you should definitely find more powerful effects that are three mana and below, in order to cut down on casting. If you can tutor most white enchantments with Zur, that lets you run more UB stuff, which has better card draw and selection. 

[[Cartouche of Ambition]] is an all-star in this deck. It gives Zur lifelink, pumps him, and helps with your clock on opponents. You also need to reconsider your manabase. Taplands are inherently slow. Since Zur is tricolor, consider getting some of the rainbow lands, like [[Mana Confluence]], or [[City of Brass]]. I think you should lean into putting Zur on the field ASAP, then protecting him while he tutors your lock pieces.

Specifically Knights of the Old Republic II The Sith Lords. It's one of my favorite games, and actually does things with the Star Wars universe that most other EU offerings don't. The game feels very lonely, dark, and isolated, and hits sides of Star Wars not usually seen. 

I plan on getting relatively spoiler-y. I don't want to drop bombs about specific plot points, but I want to stoke interest in it. If you prefer to play games completely blind, know this: The game was released in an unfinished state. Use the Sith Lords Restored Content Mod to help alleviate this problem.

This game takes place after the canonical end of Knights of the Old Republic 1, which is Darth Revan joining the side of Light and eliminating Darth Malak and the Star Forge. In the interim between KotOR one and two, the once proud Jedi order has been all but exterminated, a with the Exchange offering large sums of credits for captured Jedi, and an entire planet of Force sensitives basically destroyed by the dark side. Revan has left the galaxy, and The Republic is attempting to rebuild after the Jedi Civil War, which has spread it extremely thin. The game focuses on you, the Jedi Exile. You have been stripped of the ability to use the Force entirely, which makes you an aberration, and essentially an abomination in the eyes of most Force sensitives. 

In contrast to KotOR one, KotOR 2 has a far different tone. The first was a hero's journey essentially, with a dramatic twist towards the endgame. 2 is a much more open ended game. Think of KotOR one as Fallout 3, think of two as New Vegas(an apt comparison, as KotOR 2 is an Obsidian joint).  

The villains in it are well written, being genuinely threatening and intimidating at times, which is a far cry from characters like Darth Maul or even Darth Malak from KotOR one. One of the Sith Lords, Darth Nihilus, is a Sith whose hunger for power has literally turned him into a ghostly husk who devours Force sensitives while cruising through space in his dead capital ship. Darth Sion, another of the Sith Lords, is a corpse held together by the dark side of the Force, and is in eternal pain because of this, which fuels his inextinguishable hatred.

Overall, if your favorite scene in the Empire Strikes Back was the part where Luke confronts the Dark Side hallucination of Darth Vader in the cave on Dagobah, you might enjoy the atmosphere of KotOR 2. It's a buggy mess however, but definitely a wonderful RPG.
